claim: Sarcomeres are the force-producing units of all striated muscles.
source: Sarcomeres are the force-producing units of all striated muscles.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in muscle biology, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: In vertebrates, titin spans from the sarcomeric Z-disc to the M-band.
source: Their nanoarchitecture critically depends on the large titin protein, which in vertebrates spans from the sarcomeric Z-disc to the M-band and hence links actin and myosin filaments stably together.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about vertebrate titin structure.

claim: Titin links actin and myosin filaments stably together in vertebrates.
source: Their nanoarchitecture critically depends on the large titin protein, which in vertebrates spans from the sarcomeric Z-disc to the M-band and hence links actin and myosin filaments stably together.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about titin function.

claim: Titin ensures sarcomeric integrity in vertebrates.
source: This ensures sarcomeric integrity and determines the length of vertebrate sarcomeres.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about titin function.

claim: Titin determines the length of vertebrate sarcomeres.
source: This ensures sarcomeric integrity and determines the length of vertebrate sarcomeres.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about titin function.

claim: Sallimus bridges across the flight muscle I-band.
source: By combining nanobodies with DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy, we found that, similar to vertebrate titin, Sallimus bridges across the flight muscle I-band, whereas Projectin is located at the beginning of the A-band.
evidence: This is supported by the DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Projectin is located at the beginning of the A-band in flight muscles.
source: By combining nanobodies with DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy, we found that, similar to vertebrate titin, Sallimus bridges across the flight muscle I-band, whereas Projectin is located at the beginning of the A-band.
evidence: This is supported by the DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ends of Sallimus and Projectin overlap at the I-band/A-band border.
source: Interestingly, the ends of both proteins overlap at the I-band/A-band border, revealing a staggered organisation of the two Drosophila titin homologs.
evidence: This is supported by the DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The two Drosophila titin homologs have a staggered organisation.
source: Interestingly, the ends of both proteins overlap at the I-band/A-band border, revealing a staggered organisation of the two Drosophila titin homologs.
evidence: This is supported by the DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The staggered architecture of Sallimus and Projectin may help to stably anchor Sallimus at the myosin filament.
source: This architecture may help to stably anchor Sallimus at the myosin filament and hence ensure efficient force transduction during flight.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed staggered architecture.

claim: The staggered architecture may ensure efficient force transduction during flight.
source: This architecture may help to stably anchor Sallimus at the myosin filament and hence ensure efficient force transduction during flight.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed staggered architecture.

claim: Sarcomeres are bordered by two Z-discs.
source: Sarcomeres are bordered by two Z-discs, which anchor the plus ends of parallel actin filaments.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about sarcomere structure.

claim: Z-discs anchor the plus ends of parallel actin filaments.
source: Sarcomeres are bordered by two Z-discs, which anchor the plus ends of parallel actin filaments.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about sarcomere structure.

claim: In vertebrate sarcomeres, titin's N-terminus is anchored to α-actinin at the Z-disc.
source: In vertebrate sarcomeres, actin and myosin filaments are mechanically linked by the connecting filament built by the gigantic titin protein, whose N-terminus is anchored to α-actinin at the Z-disc while its C-terminus is embedded within the sarcomeric M-band.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In vertebrate sarcomeres, titin's C-terminus is embedded within the sarcomeric M-band.
source: In vertebrate sarcomeres, actin and myosin filaments are mechanically linked by the connecting filament built by the gigantic titin protein, whose N-terminus is anchored to α-actinin at the Z-disc while its C-terminus is embedded within the sarcomeric M-band.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Titin spans as a linear protein across half a sarcomere in vertebrate muscle.
source: Thus, titin spans as a linear protein across half a sarcomere in vertebrate muscle (Gautel and Djinović-Carugo, 2016; Lange et al., 2006; Linke, 2018; Squire et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The sarcomere length in relaxed human skeletal muscle is about 3 µm.
source: This stereotypic sarcomere architecture results in a defined sarcomere length (distance between two neighbouring Z-discs), which is about 3 µm in relaxed human skeletal muscle (Ehler and Gautel, 2008; Llewellyn et al., 2008; Regev et al., 2011), and is responsible for the typical striated appearance of skeletal muscles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Deletion of parts of titin's flexible I-band in mouse skeletal muscle resulted in a shortening of the sarcomeric I-band.
source: Deletion of parts of titin's flexible I-band or its stiff A-band regions in mouse skeletal muscle resulted in a shortening of the sarcomeric I-band or A-band, respectively (Brynnel et al., 2018; Tonino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published genetic studies.

claim: Deletion of parts of titin's stiff A-band regions in mouse skeletal muscle resulted in a shortening of the sarcomeric A-band.
source: Deletion of parts of titin's flexible I-band or its stiff A-band regions in mouse skeletal muscle resulted in a shortening of the sarcomeric I-band or A-band, respectively (Brynnel et al., 2018; Tonino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published genetic studies.

claim: Titin is the main sarcomeric component responsible for the passive tension of the muscle.
source: Furthermore, recent evidence substantiated that titin is the main sarcomeric component responsible for the passive tension of the muscle, suggesting that mechanical tension present in relaxed muscle is stretching titin into its extended conformation (Li et al., 2020; Linke, 2018; Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020; Swist et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Mechanical tension present in relaxed muscle is stretching titin into its extended conformation.
source: Furthermore, recent evidence substantiated that titin is the main sarcomeric component responsible for the passive tension of the muscle, suggesting that mechanical tension present in relaxed muscle is stretching titin into its extended conformation (Li et al., 2020; Linke, 2018; Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020; Swist et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature and represents an inference from those studies.

claim: Titin mechanically links actin and myosin filaments together in vertebrate striated muscle.
source: Thus, titin mechanically links actin and myosin filaments together and is responsible for establishing and maintaining sarcomeric architecture in vertebrate striated muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited evidence about titin's structure and function.

claim: Titin is responsible for establishing and maintaining sarcomeric architecture in vertebrate striated muscle.
source: Thus, titin mechanically links actin and myosin filaments together and is responsible for establishing and maintaining sarcomeric architecture in vertebrate striated muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited evidence about titin's structure and function.

claim: In Drosophila and Caenorhabditis elegans, titin's role appears to be split in two proteins.
source: However, in contrast to vertebrates, titin's role in Drosophila and Caenorhabditis elegans appears to be split in two proteins, one containing the flexible I-band features and the other the stiff A-band features of titin (Flaherty et al., 2002; Loreau et al., 2023; Porto et al., 2021; Tskhovrebova and Trinick, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The sarcomere length in Drosophila indirect flight muscles is about 3.5 µm.
source: In Drosophila, the sarcomere length is about 3.5 µm for indirect flight muscles and about 8 µm for larval body wall muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila muscle structure.

claim: The sarcomere length in Drosophila larval body wall muscles is about 8 µm.
source: In Drosophila, the sarcomere length is about 3.5 µm for indirect flight muscles and about 8 µm for larval body wall muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila muscle structure.

claim: The majority of stiffness in Drosophila flight muscles is due to Sallimus.
source: The majority of this stiffness is due to Sls in flight muscles (Kulke et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A large part of the flexible spring domains encoded in sls and bent are skipped by alternative splicing in flight muscles.
source: To achieve this high stiffness, a large part of the flexible spring domains encoded in both titin gene homologs sls and bent (bt; protein name: Projectin) are skipped by alternative splicing (Ayme-Southgate et al., 2005; Bullard et al., 2005; Burkart et al., 2007; Spletter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The PEVK spring domains are largely spliced out in adult flight muscles in both sls and bent genes.
source: We verified that in both genes the flexible PEVK spring domains are largely spliced out in adult flight muscles; however, their more 3′-located exons are present at least in some longer isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of transcriptomics data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Both N-terminal anti-Sls nanobodies result in single bands at the Z-discs in flight muscles when observed with confocal microscopy.
source: In flight muscles, both N-terminal anti-Sls nanobodies, namely, Sls-Nano2 (binding Sls-Ig13/14) as well as C-terminal anti-Sls nanobodies, namely, Sls-Nano42 (binding to SlsIg51/52), result in single bands at the Z-discs when coupled to fluorescent dyes and observed with confocal microscopy (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: C-terminal anti-Sls nanobodies result in single bands at the Z-discs in flight muscles when observed with confocal microscopy.
source: In flight muscles, both N-terminal anti-Sls nanobodies, namely, Sls-Nano2 (binding Sls-Ig13/14) as well as C-terminal anti-Sls nanobodies, namely, Sls-Nano42 (binding to SlsIg51/52), result in single bands at the Z-discs when coupled to fluorescent dyes and observed with confocal microscopy (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: N-terminal anti-Projectin nanobodies each result in one band at the Z-disc in flight muscles.
source: Similarly, N-terminal anti-Projectin nanobodies, here Proj-Nano30 (recognising Proj-Ig5-8) and Proj-Nano29 (binding Proj-Fn1-2), each result in one band at the Z-disc (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nanobodies against C-terminally located Projectin domains result in two bands at large distances from the Z-disc.
source: In contrast, nanobodies against C-terminally located Projectin domains, here Proj-Nano33 (binding Proj-Ig27-Fn35) and Proj-Nano37 (binding the Projectin kinase domain), result in two bands at large distances from the Z-disc (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Projectin is present in an extended conformation in flight muscles.
source: These data demonstrate that Projectin is present in an extended conformation, and since the flight muscle I-band extends less than 100 nm from the Z-disc (Burkart et al., 2007; Kronert et al., 2018; Loison et al., 2018; Reedy and Beall, 1993; Szikora et al., 2020), a large part of Projectin is present along the myosin filament.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed band positions and cited literature about I-band length.

claim: A large part of Projectin is present along the myosin filament in flight muscles.
source: These data demonstrate that Projectin is present in an extended conformation, and since the flight muscle I-band extends less than 100 nm from the Z-disc (Burkart et al., 2007; Kronert et al., 2018; Loison et al., 2018; Reedy and Beall, 1993; Szikora et al., 2020), a large part of Projectin is present along the myosin filament.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed band positions and cited literature about I-band length.

claim: The flight muscle I-band extends less than 100 nm from the Z-disc.
source: These data demonstrate that Projectin is present in an extended conformation, and since the flight muscle I-band extends less than 100 nm from the Z-disc (Burkart et al., 2007; Kronert et al., 2018; Loison et al., 2018; Reedy and Beall, 1993; Szikora et al., 2020), a large part of Projectin is present along the myosin filament.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Sls-Ig13/14 is localised about 50 nm away from the centre of the Z-disc.
source: Our results verified that Sls-Ig13/14 is localised about 50 nm away from the centre of the Z-disc and that Sls-Ig51/Fn2 is about 50 nm farther towards the middle of the sarcomere (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sls-Ig51/Fn2 is about 50 nm farther towards the middle of the sarcomere than Sls-Ig13/14.
source: Our results verified that Sls-Ig13/14 is localised about 50 nm away from the centre of the Z-disc and that Sls-Ig51/Fn2 is about 50 nm farther towards the middle of the sarcomere (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sls is bridging across the entire sarcomeric I-band with its N-terminus anchored within the Z-disc and its C-terminal end reaching the myosin filament.
source: Since the I-band of flight muscles is less than 100 nm from the Z-disc (Burkart et al., 2007; Kronert et al., 2018; Loison et al., 2018; Reedy and Beall, 1993; Szikora et al., 2020), this strongly suggests that Sls is bridging across the entire sarcomeric I-band with its N-terminus anchored within the Z-disc and its C-terminal end reaching the myosin filament.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured positions and cited literature about I-band length.

claim: Sls could mechanically link the Z-disc to the myosin filament in the flight muscles, similar to the long vertebrate titin.
source: Thus, Sls could mechanically link the Z-disc to the myosin filament in the flight muscles, similar to the long vertebrate titin.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed architecture and comparison to vertebrate titin.

claim: The N-terminus of Projectin is about 100 nm away from the Z-disc.
source: Since we found that the N-terminus of Projectin is also about 100 nm away from the Z-disc and thus located at the beginning of the thick filament (Figure 4A), we wanted to further investigate the precise orientation of the Projectin N-terminal domains.
evidence: This is supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The N-terminus of Projectin is located at the beginning of the thick filament.
source: Since we found that the N-terminus of Projectin is also about 100 nm away from the Z-disc and thus located at the beginning of the thick filament (Figure 4A), we wanted to further investigate the precise orientation of the Projectin N-terminal domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured position and known sarcomere structure.

claim: The average distance between Proj-Ig5/8 and Pro-Fn1/2 epitopes is about 25 nm.
source: To do so, we performed two-colour DNA-PAINT to localise Proj-Ig5/8 (with Proj-Nano30) and Pro-Fn1/2 (with Proj-Nano29) in the same sarcomere and found an average distance between the two epitopes of about 25 nm, with Proj-Ig5-8 being always closer to the Z-disc relative to Proj-Fn1/2 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by two-colour DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Proj-Ig5-8 is always closer to the Z-disc relative to Proj-Fn1/2.
source: To do so, we performed two-colour DNA-PAINT to localise Proj-Ig5/8 (with Proj-Nano30) and Pro-Fn1/2 (with Proj-Nano29) in the same sarcomere and found an average distance between the two epitopes of about 25 nm, with Proj-Ig5-8 being always closer to the Z-disc relative to Proj-Fn1/2 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by two-colour DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Proj-Ig27-Fn35 epitope is located 350 nm away from the Z-disc.
source: Consistently, the more C-terminally located Proj-Ig27-Fn35 epitope is located far into the myosin filament that begins at 100 nm (Szikora et al., 2020), being 350 nm away from the Z-disc (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by two-colour DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The N-terminal part of Projectin is arranged in an extended, likely linear conformation reaching from the myosin filament into the I-band.
source: This strongly suggests that the N-terminal part of Projectin is arranged in an extended, likely linear conformation reaching from the myosin filament into the I-band and thus running in parallel to the C-terminal domains of Sls.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured positions of Projectin domains.

claim: The N-terminal part of Projectin runs in parallel to the C-terminal domains of Sls.
source: This strongly suggests that the N-terminal part of Projectin is arranged in an extended, likely linear conformation reaching from the myosin filament into the I-band and thus running in parallel to the C-terminal domains of Sls.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured positions of Projectin and Sls domains.

claim: Proj-Nano29 is about 15 nm farther from the Z-disc than Sls-Nano39 in all sarcomeres measured.
source: Interestingly, we found that in all sarcomeres measured, the Proj-Nano29 is about 15 nm farther from the Z-disc than Sls-Nano39, whereas, in 42 out of 45 sarcomeres investigated, Proj-Nano30 is on average 7–8 nm closer to the Z-disc than Sls-Nano42 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by two-colour DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In 42 out of 45 sarcomeres investigated, Proj-Nano30 is on average 7–8 nm closer to the Z-disc than Sls-Nano42.
source: Interestingly, we found that in all sarcomeres measured, the Proj-Nano29 is about 15 nm farther from the Z-disc than Sls-Nano39, whereas, in 42 out of 45 sarcomeres investigated, Proj-Nano30 is on average 7–8 nm closer to the Z-disc than Sls-Nano42 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by two-colour DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There is a significant overlap of the linear Sls and Projectin proteins at the I-band/A-band interface.
source: Our data enabled us to build a molecular map of the Drosophila titin homologs in flight muscle sarcomeres, which revealed a significant overlap of the linear Sls and Projectin proteins at the I-band/A-band interface as visualised in a 'composite sarcomere' reconstructed by imaging flight muscles from six different hemi-thoraces (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the composite data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The distance between the measured epitopes is constant despite variable sarcomere length.
source: This strategy is valid as we found that although our mounting protocol for TIRF imaging results in a slightly variable sarcomere length of around 3.5 µm (Spletter et al., 2015), the distance between the measured epitopes is constant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal Proj-Ig5-8 epitope is located 90 nm from the Z-disc.
source: Pooling all data verified that the N-terminal Proj-Ig5-8 epitope is located 90 nm from the Z-disc, whereas the C-terminal Sls epitopes Sls-Ig49/50 and Sls-Ig51-Fn2 are located about 98 nm from the Z-disc.
evidence: This is supported by pooled DNA-PAINT data from all experiments.

claim: The C-terminal Sls epitopes Sls-Ig49/50 and Sls-Ig51-Fn2 are located about 98 nm from the Z-disc.
source: Pooling all data verified that the N-terminal Proj-Ig5-8 epitope is located 90 nm from the Z-disc, whereas the C-terminal Sls epitopes Sls-Ig49/50 and Sls-Ig51-Fn2 are located about 98 nm from the Z-disc.
evidence: This is supported by pooled DNA-PAINT data from all experiments.

claim: The staggered linear organisation of Sallimus and Projectin suggests a mechanism to mechanically link the sarcomeric Z-disc in insect flight muscle with the myosin filament.
source: This is consistent with a staggered linear organisation of Sallimus and Projectin, which suggests an attractive mechanism how to mechanically link the sarcomeric Z-disc in insect flight muscle with the myosin filament using both titin homologs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed staggered architecture.

claim: Nanobodies are very efficient in penetrating large flight muscle fibres containing highly packed sarcomeres.
source: We have shown that our nanobodies are also very efficient in penetrating the large flight muscle fibres containing highly packed sarcomeres (Loreau et al., 2023), which are amongst the most protein-dense macromolecular structures in biology (Daneshparvar et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the successful staining results and citations.

claim: Flight muscle sarcomeres are amongst the most protein-dense macromolecular structures in biology.
source: We have shown that our nanobodies are also very efficient in penetrating the large flight muscle fibres containing highly packed sarcomeres (Loreau et al., 2023), which are amongst the most protein-dense macromolecular structures in biology (Daneshparvar et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The location of Sls-Ig16 is about 50 nm from the centre of the Z-disc.
source: This included the Sls-Ig16 antibody, locating Sls-Ig16 about 50 nm from the centre of the Z-disc (Szikora et al., 2020), which is in good agreement with the location of Sls-Ig13/14 we found here.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous STORM study.

claim: The Z-disc components α-Actinin and Zasp52 extend only about 35 nm from the centre of the Z-disc.
source: This study further showed that the Z-disc components α-Actinin and Zasp52 extend only about 35 nm from the centre of the Z-disc, whereas Filamin stretches with its C-term to about 55 nm (Szikora et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous STORM study.

claim: Filamin stretches with its C-terminus to about 55 nm from the centre of the Z-disc.
source: This study further showed that the Z-disc components α-Actinin and Zasp52 extend only about 35 nm from the centre of the Z-disc, whereas Filamin stretches with its C-term to about 55 nm (Szikora et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous STORM study.

claim: The N-terminus of Sls can reach and interact with Z-disc components including α-Actinin, Zasp52, and possibly Filamin.
source: This strongly suggests that the N-terminus of Sls, with its remaining 12 Ig domains, can reach and interact with these Z-disc components and possibly also with Filamin, as has been reported biochemically (González-Morales et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured positions and cited biochemical studies.

claim: The C-terminal end of Sls is located about 100 nm from the centre of the Z-disc in flight muscles.
source: Thus, it is insightful that our newly developed C-terminal Sls nanobodies show that the C-terminal end of Sls is located about 100 nm from the centre of the Z-disc in flight muscles.
evidence: This is supported by the DNA-PAINT data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Myosin filaments begin about 100 nm from the centre of the Z-disc in flight muscles.
source: Although we have not imaged myosin directly in our samples, both STORM and electron-microscopy studies demonstrated that myosin filaments begin about 100 nm from the centre of the Z-disc, making the half I-band less than 100 nm wide (Burkart et al., 2007; Kronert et al., 2018; Loison et al., 2018; Reedy and Beall, 1993; Szikora et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous STORM and electron microscopy studies.

claim: Sls is spanning across the short flight muscle I-band and could interact through its C-terminal domains with the myosin filament.
source: This strongly suggests that, as in vertebrates, Sls is indeed spanning across the short flight muscle I-band, where it could interact through its C-terminal domains with the myosin filament and hence could mechanically link the Z-disc with the myosin filament.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured positions and comparison to vertebrate titin.

claim: The long isoform of the C. elegans titin homolog TTN-1 bridges across the I-band reaching the beginning of the A-band in C. elegans body muscles.
source: Interestingly, the long isoform of the C. elegans titin homolog TTN-1 was shown to also bridge across the I-band reaching the beginning of the A-band in C. elegans body muscles and in vitro studies demonstrated that its C-terminal Ig38-40 domains indeed bind to myosin with low nanomolar affinity (Forbes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The C-terminal Ig38-40 domains of C. elegans TTN-1 bind to myosin with low nanomolar affinity.
source: Interestingly, the long isoform of the C. elegans titin homolog TTN-1 was shown to also bridge across the I-band reaching the beginning of the A-band in C. elegans body muscles and in vitro studies demonstrated that its C-terminal Ig38-40 domains indeed bind to myosin with low nanomolar affinity (Forbes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Drosophila Sls may interact with myosin or Projectin and function as an I-band ruler in insect muscles.
source: These data are consistent with our hypothesis that Drosophila Sls may interact with myosin or Projectin and thus function as an I-band ruler in insect muscles (see model in Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed architecture and comparison to other systems.

claim: A chain of 40 Ig domains would result in a length of about 160 nm.
source: As the length of an isolated Ig domain is about 4 nm (Mayans et al., 2001), a chain of 40 Ig domains, which are present in the flight muscle Sls isoforms that we studied here, would result in a length of about 160 nm instead of the observed 100 nm.
evidence: This is a calculation based on cited structural data and the observed number of domains.

claim: The Sls native structure in close proximity to actin filaments in the flight muscle I-band might be more complex than a straight linear array of Ig domains.
source: Hence, the Sls native structure in close proximity to actin filaments present in the flight muscle I-band might be more complex than a straight linear array of Ig domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between calculated and observed lengths.

claim: Non-flight muscles like leg, jump, and larval muscles express longer versions of Sls that include the large and flexible PEVK domains.
source: The interpretation that Sls length rules I-band length is also supported by the observation that non-flight muscles like leg, jump, and larval muscles, which contain long I-bands, do express longer versions of Sls that include the large and flexible PEVK domains (Burkart et al., 2007; Spletter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Sls is more than 2 µm long in larval muscles.
source: Indeed, in the accompanying paper using the Sls nanobodies, we showed that Sls is more than 2 µm long in larval muscles to bridge over these long I-bands (Loreau et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the accompanying paper.

claim: Sls determines I-band length in different muscle types.
source: This strongly suggests that Sls determines I-band length in the different muscle types; however, a direct genetic test that modifies Sls length and assays I-band length remains to be done.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between Sls length and I-band length, but acknowledged as requiring further genetic testing.

claim: Projectin starts about 90 nm from the Z-disc in Drosophila flight muscles.
source: Interestingly, we demonstrate that in Drosophila flight muscles, Projectin, which is very similar to the A-band part of vertebrate titin, with long Ig-Fn super-repeats and a C-terminal kinase domain, starts about 90 nm from the Z-disc.
evidence: This is supported by the DNA-PAINT data presented in the manuscript.

claim: It is very unlikely that Projectin can interact with Z-disc components directly.
source: Hence, it is very unlikely that it can interact with Z-disc components directly as these are far from the N-terminal end of Projectin (model in Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured distance between Projectin's N-terminus and Z-disc components.

claim: The N-terminus of Projectin is sticking into the flight muscle I-band.
source: Our precise distance measurements suggest that the N-terminus of Projectin, which does contain a series of Ig domains, typical for the I-band part of titin, is sticking into the flight muscle I-band, whereas its first Fn/Ig super-repeat is located at beginning of the A-band (110 nm from the Z-disc) and hence can interact with myosin, as can its remaining Ig-Fn super-repeats that extend over a length of about 250 nm towards the M-band.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured positions of Projectin domains.

claim: Projectin's first Fn/Ig super-repeat is located at beginning of the A-band (110 nm from the Z-disc).
source: Our precise distance measurements suggest that the N-terminus of Projectin, which does contain a series of Ig domains, typical for the I-band part of titin, is sticking into the flight muscle I-band, whereas its first Fn/Ig super-repeat is located at beginning of the A-band (110 nm from the Z-disc) and hence can interact with myosin, as can its remaining Ig-Fn super-repeats that extend over a length of about 250 nm towards the M-band.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured positions of Projectin domains.

claim: Projectin's Ig-Fn super-repeats extend over a length of about 250 nm towards the M-band.
source: Our precise distance measurements suggest that the N-terminus of Projectin, which does contain a series of Ig domains, typical for the I-band part of titin, is sticking into the flight muscle I-band, whereas its first Fn/Ig super-repeat is located at beginning of the A-band (110 nm from the Z-disc) and hence can interact with myosin, as can its remaining Ig-Fn super-repeats that extend over a length of about 250 nm towards the M-band.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured positions of Projectin domains.

claim: The Projectin kinase localises in a sharp band far from the M-band.
source: This localisation differs somewhat from what was found by STORM of dissected myofibrils which placed the Ig domain 26 of Projectin only about 70 nm from the Z-disc (Szikora et al., 2020). We found that the Projectin kinase localises in a sharp band; however, it remains far from the M-band.
evidence: This is supported by the DNA-PAINT data presented in the manuscript.

claim: It is hard to imagine that Projectin alone can directly rule the A-band length of flight muscle sarcomeres.
source: Hence, it is hard to imagine that Projectin alone can directly rule the A-band length of flight muscle sarcomeres as it is only present at its distal ends, spanning about 15% of the myosin filament.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed limited span of Projectin along the myosin filament.

claim: Drosophila flight muscles are very stiff to effectively power wing oscillations during flight at 200 Hz.
source: Drosophila flight muscles are very stiff to effectively power wing oscillations during flight at 200 Hz.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila flight muscle physiology.

claim: Contraction of the DVMs moves the wings up and stretches the DLMs to induce their contraction.
source: The perpendicular arrangement of the antagonistic dorsoventral (DVMs) versus the dorso-longitudinal flight muscles (DLMs) enables an effective stretch-activation mechanism as trigger: contraction of the DVMs moves the wings up and stretches the DLMs to induce their contraction, which will move the wings down again for the next cycle (Dickinson et al., 2005; Pringle, 1981; Syme and Josephson, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on flight muscle mechanics.

claim: Flight muscles express a particular troponin C isoform (TpnC4) which requires to be stretched to displace tropomyosin from myosin binding sites on actin filaments.
source: The importance of strain in these muscles is highlighted by their expression of a particular troponin C isoform (TpnC4), which requires to be stretched to displace tropomyosin from myosin binding sites on actin filaments (Agianian et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Myosin experiences a stretch-induced deformation before effective actin binding and maximum force production in flight muscles.
source: Furthermore, myosin also experiences a stretch-induced deformation before effective actin binding and maximum force production (Iwamoto and Yagi, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Drosophila sarcomeres contractions have a peak-to-peak amplitude of about 3.5% or 60 nm per half sarcomere during flight.
source: Drosophila sarcomeres contractions have a peak-to-peak amplitude of about 3.5% or 60 nm per half sarcomere during flight (measured in Drosophila virilis; Chan and Dickinson, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Insect flight muscles can produce up to 110 W/kg power output.
source: This 3.5% strain is needed to produce the up to 110 W/kg power output of insect flight muscles (Chan and Dickinson, 1996), which is consistent with the hypothesis that strain across molecules stores the elastic energy for the next contraction cycle in Drosophila (Dickinson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Sls is a perfect candidate for storing elastic energy during flight muscle oscillations.
source: A perfect candidate for such a molecule is Sls as it bridges across the I-band, which likely changes length during the fast contraction cycles.
evidence: This is an inference based on Sls's position and the mechanics of muscle contraction.

claim: Sls length would oscillate during flight, which likely results in high oscillating forces across Sls.
source: Thus, Sls length would oscillate during flight, which likely results in high oscillating forces across Sls during flight.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanics of muscle contraction and Sls's position.

claim: The staggered architecture of Sls and Projectin might be required to effectively anchor Sls to the myosin filament and to prevent sarcomere rupturing during flight.
source: The precise linear arrangement of Projectin at the beginning of the myosin filament and the found overlap with Sls suggests that this staggered architecture of Sls and Proj might be required to effectively anchor Sls to the myosin filament and to prevent sarcomere rupturing during flight.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed architecture.

claim: Flight-induced muscle ruptures are generated when muscle attachment to tendons is weakened.
source: Such flight-induced muscle ruptures are generated when muscle attachment to tendons is weakened, underscoring the high muscle forces and high strain produced during flight (Lemke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Projectin may serve as an effective glue to stably connect Sls to the myosin filament.
source: Projectin may thus serve as an effective glue to stably connect Sls to the myosin filament.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed overlap of Sls and Projectin.

claim: Both Sls and Projectin are needed to assemble contractile sarcomeres in Drosophila larval muscles.
source: This is also consistent with the findings that both Sls and Projectin are needed to assemble contractile sarcomeres in Drosophila larval muscles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Knockdown of either Sls or Projectin results in embryonic lethality and defective sarcomerogenesis.
source: Knockdown of either protein results in embryonic lethality and defective sarcomerogenesis (Loreau et al., 2023; Schnorrer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The staggered architecture of the two Drosophila titin homologs may effectively allow force transduction and ensure the mechanical integrity of flight muscles sarcomeres.
source: Taken together, the staggered architecture of the two Drosophila titin homologs may effectively allow force transduction and ensure the mechanical integrity of flight muscles sarcomeres, both very prominent functions of mammalian titin (Li et al., 2020; Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020; Swist et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed architecture and comparison to mammalian titin.

claim: DNA-PAINT enables imaging at particularly high spatial resolution.
source: To resolve the relative localisation of Sls and Projectin, we turned our attention to super-resolution imaging with DNA-PAINT as it enables imaging at particularly high spatial resolution (Jungmann et al., 2014; Lelek et al., 2021; Schnitzbauer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on DNA-PAINT.

claim: The localisation precision of DNA-PAINT in this study was estimated between 4 and 8 nm using the NeNA metric.
source: First, the localisations were detected by a threshold-based detection and fitted with a least-square fit; the resulting localisation precision was estimated between 4 and 8 nm using the NeNA metric (Endesfelder et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis methods and citation to the NeNA metric.

claim: The 95% confidence intervals for epitope positions were only 1–8 nm.
source: Hence, the localisation of the different Sls and Projectin domains investigated using all sarcomeres measured resulted in a very high localisation precision with 95% confidence intervals of only 1–8 nm (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the bootstrapping analysis shown in Figure 6B.
